what: Ligand Pharmaceuticals buys royalties on medicines. Rather than discovering or selling drugs itself, it funds development or acquires existing royalty rights, then collects a percentage of sales when the medicine reaches the market. It also licenses drug formulation technologies that other companies use in their own products.
customers: It has no patients or prescribers. Its counterparties are pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies that need funding or formulation technology, and its income is a share of their product sales.
money: A percentage of sales of approved medicines in which Ligand holds royalty rights.
Sales of its formulation technology and milestone payments from partners.
moat: A royalty is the best structure in pharmaceuticals: the holder gets the upside of a successful medicine without paying for the clinical trials that fail or the sales force that sells it. Ligand’s advantage is in selecting which royalties to buy — a judgement business rather than an operating one, with almost no fixed costs between revenue and profit.
risks: The shares trade at about 115.2 times earnings, 22.6 times sales and 106.6 times EV/EBITDA — an extremely full price on $253.8M of revenue.
Revenue has been volatile, falling from $241.5M in 2021 to $131.3M in 2023 before recovering to $268.1M in 2025, because royalty income depends on partners’ products.
A royalty on a medicine that fails in trials or loses market share is worth nothing, and the losses are permanent rather than cyclical.
Patent expiry eventually ends every royalty, so the portfolio has to be continuously replenished simply to stand still.
Eleven analysts average a $361.27 target against a $286.94 price, which still assumes the pipeline delivers.
opportunities: A net margin of 46.4% shows the model: there is very little between royalty revenue and profit.
Cash of $733.5M against $451.5M of debt gives a net cash position and the capacity to buy more royalties.
Free cash flow of $90.6M on $253.8M of revenue is strong, and does not require any operating infrastructure.
Royalties on approved medicines are contractual income that does not depend on Ligand doing anything further.
The formulation technology business generates recurring revenue and brings Ligand into contact with partners whose royalties it might buy.
watch: New royalty acquisitions and the clinical progress of the underlying medicines. The existing royalties pay automatically; everything that determines future value happens in what gets bought and whether those drugs succeed.
view: Royalty businesses in pharmaceuticals are structurally attractive for the same reason as in mining: the holder captures the upside and pays none of the costs. Ligand does not run clinical trials, does not employ a sales force and does not manufacture anything. It buys a percentage of someone else’s product sales. The 46.4% net margin is simply what that looks like in the accounts, and there is very little between revenue and profit because there is very little to pay for.

The skill in the business is selection, and it is worth being honest that this is almost impossible to assess from outside. A royalty on a medicine that succeeds is enormously valuable; a royalty on one that fails a trial or loses share to a competitor is worth nothing, and the loss is permanent. Ligand’s revenue history shows this plainly — $241 million in 2021, down to $131 million in 2023, back to $268 million in 2025. That volatility is not operational; it is the portfolio’s underlying medicines performing or not.

There is also a structural treadmill that gets overlooked. Every pharmaceutical royalty ends at patent expiry, which means the portfolio must be continuously replenished just to hold revenue flat. Ligand’s $734 million of cash against $452 million of debt gives it the capacity to do that, and the formulation technology business usefully puts it in contact with exactly the companies whose royalties it might want to buy. But the requirement to keep buying never stops.

What stops me is the price. At 115 times earnings, 22.6 times sales and 107 times EV/EBITDA on $254 million of revenue, you are paying for pipeline outcomes that have not happened, in a business where individual outcomes are binary and the portfolio is not large enough to average them out. The model is excellent and the multiple assumes the selection skill is proven and repeatable, which is a much stronger claim than the revenue history supports. I would want to see several more years of acquisitions performing before paying this.
bull: Royalties on medicines already approved keep compounding while new acquisitions and pipeline milestones land, and a near-costless model turns revenue almost entirely into profit.
bear: A key underlying medicine fails or loses share, patent expiries outpace new royalty purchases, and 115 times earnings on $254 million of revenue has nowhere to fall but down.
